title: Open Hearts and a Mismatched Yoke
sum: Paul finishes his long defense of his ministry (2:14-6:10) with an appeal and a list. The appeal: do not let God's grace come to nothing; Isaiah's "day of salvation" is now (6:1-2). The list: nine hardships, eight virtues and seven pairs of opposites, each saying how a servant of God looks to the world and how he really is (6:3-10). It is Paul's letter of recommendation, written in scars.

Then the tone turns tender. His mouth and heart are "wide open" to the Corinthians; they are the ones who are cramped (6:11-13). Next comes a block of five sharp questions and a chain of Old Testament promises: do not be yoked with unbelievers, because you are God's temple (6:14-18). The passage runs on into 7:1. Scholars are divided on whether it was part of the letter at first; this page sets out the views.
readings: Read as a call to leave idol worship

Corinth was full of temples and dining rooms where the city's meals and parties were held in the presence of the gods. Paul has already told the church not to share the "table of demons" (1 Corinthians 10:14-22). On this reading the 'yoke' is a shared religious life with unbelievers, and 6:14-7:1 is the same warning in the language of Israel's covenant. The title of Webb's study places the paragraph in the letter's new-covenant and second-exodus setting.
Read as a call to separate in close ties

Teachers across the centuries have applied the verse to marriage with non-Christians, to business partnerships, to membership in lodges and clubs, and to churches that join with groups that deny the faith. Paul's own letters (1 Corinthians 7:12-16; 10:27) leave those applications open and also limit them: he did not require believers married to unbelievers to leave, and he did not forbid eating with unbelievers.
Read as a piece from outside the letter

Some scholars hold that the paragraph did not begin with Paul. Betz (1973) asked in the title of his article whether it is an anti-Pauline fragment. On such views the 'unbelievers' may be Gentiles or Jews outside the community, and the paragraph should not be read as Paul's answer to Corinth. The question is open, and this page does not count heads.

views.H: Paul writes from Macedonia in the mid-50s, soon after Titus brought news that most of the church had turned back to him (7:5-7). Corinth was a Roman colony rebuilt in 44 BC, rich, status-conscious and full of temples; Paul's hardships in 6:4-5 can be matched with Acts (13:50; 14:19; 16:22-24; 19:23-41). A city of that kind valued honor and a good reputation, which makes the list at 6:8-10 (dishonor, slander, being 'unknown') a deliberate reversal of its values. 'Now is the day of salvation' is the verse the Roman church later read on Ash Wednesday.
views.C: Is 6:14-7:1 part of the letter? For a break: 7:2 continues 6:13 smoothly; several words in it appear nowhere else in the New Testament (by this site's word data); and the paragraph says 'unbelievers' where the rest of the letter speaks of opponents. For unity: Paul uses digressions and the topic suits Corinth. The question is open. See the deep dive.
views.L: The hardships list is a model of ancient style: nine items in three triples (pressures, violence, chosen hardships), then virtues, then seven 'as... and yet' contrasts. The pairs are a chiasm-like arrangement of reputation (honor/dishonor), truth (impostors/true), fame (unknown/known), life and death, grief and joy, poverty and wealth. Verses 11-13 turn on the pun of 'wide' and 'cramped,' which links back to 'distresses' (6:4). The five questions of 6:14-16 all expect the answer 'none,' and the Old Testament chain in 6:16-18 is introduced as one speech of God.
views.J: Isaiah 49:8 and 52:11, Leviticus 26:11-12, Ezekiel 20 and 37 and 2 Samuel 7:14 are all Israel's texts about return and God's presence. A Jewish reader hears Paul say that these promises are coming true among Gentiles in Christ, which Paul's own Jewish contemporaries would have seen as unusual. The mismatched yoke itself comes from Torah (Deuteronomy 22:10; Leviticus 19:19).
views.T: Tertullian, in To His Wife, book 2, argues against marrying unbelievers (he does not cite this verse there). The card shows how the Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed churches treat marriage with unbelievers, and how the Schleitheim Confession (1527), article 4, calls for separation from the world. See the card.

deep.h: The case for and against an interpolation in 6:14-7:1
deep.b:
The break. Read 6:11-13 and then 7:2: "Our heart has grown wide... Give us room." The two fit like halves. Between them 6:14-7:1 changes subject and tone, from a personal appeal to a command about separation, and its words are unusual for Paul: heterozygeo, metoche, synkatathesis and molysmos are found nowhere else in the New Testament (by this site's word data), and "flesh and spirit" as two sides of defilement (7:1) is not Paul's usual use of 'flesh.'

The arguments. Those who doubt that Paul wrote the paragraph for this place point to the break between 6:13 and 7:2 and to the unusual words. Betz asked in the title of his 1973 article whether it is an anti-Pauline fragment. Those who defend it say that Paul wrote on a new topic here, so new words are expected; that the paragraph uses Old Testament texts in the way Paul does elsewhere (Romans 9:25-26; 2 Corinthians 3); that it fits Corinth, where the warning about idol temples had already been given (1 Corinthians 10:14-22); that it belongs with the 'second exodus' and new-covenant themes of the letter (the title of Webb's study); and that Paul often interrupts himself. The jump from 6:13 to 7:2 is real, but it can also be read as a deliberate pause that makes the return more tender.

The main positions. (1) Paul wrote the paragraph for this letter as it stands (Webb; the title of Fee's article says it is about food offered to idols, as in 1 Corinthians 8-10). (2) Paul wrote it on another occasion, for example as part of an earlier letter, and it was placed here later. (3) Paul took up and adapted an existing Jewish or Jewish-Christian text, those who hold this differ on whether Paul or a later editor put it here. (4) Someone other than Paul wrote it and a later editor added it (the title of Betz's article asks this).

Where this leaves a reader. The question is open, and this page does not count heads. Whichever way it goes, the paragraph stands in this letter as we have it, and this site's Plain translates it in place.

Paul sets five pairs against each other: righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness, Christ and Beliar, believer and unbeliever, God's temple and idols. Each pair is two things that cannot share a house. Beliar is a form of the Hebrew Belial, 'worthless' (see the note on 6:15).

A common reader's question is whether this is Paul's usual way of speaking about the world. It is partly: Romans 13:12 speaks of the works of darkness and the armor of light, and 1 Thessalonians 5:4-8 of children of light. But Paul also does not shrink from living among unbelievers (1 Corinthians 5:10), so the dualism is about worship and allegiance, not geography.

deep.title: A reading to test: 'distress' and 'cramped' make one frame
deep.b: The root stenochoria ('narrow place') appears in the hardships (6:4), in 4:8 ("pressed but not cramped") and in 6:12 ("cramped in your own feelings"). I suggest that Paul has deliberately framed 6:4-13 on this pair: he has been through every narrow place and is wide; they are in no outward narrow place and are cramped. It is a small observation, but it makes the rhetoric of 6:11-13 a reply to 6:4-10, not just a transition. Commentators note the verbal link but I know of none who build on it. It rests on 2 Corinthians 4:8, 6:4 and 6:11-12.

echoes: Isaiah 49:8; Isaiah 52:11; Psalm 118:18; Leviticus 26:11-12; Ezekiel 37:27; Ezekiel 20:34; 2 Samuel 7:14; Deuteronomy 22:10; 1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 4:9-13; 1 Corinthians 10:14-22; Romans 8:35

settings.to: the church at Corinth, a mostly Gentile congregation in the capital of the province of Achaia, meeting in several houses
settings.when: from Macedonia, in the mid-50s AD, after Titus's good report (7:5-7) and as Paul turns to the last charges against him
settings.why: to finish the defense of his ministry (2:14-6:10) with an appeal that carries the reconciliation of 5:18-21 to its point: do not take God's grace for nothing. The list of hardships is his answer to the demand for letters of recommendation (3:1): he points to what his service has cost. Knowing the Corinthian love of status makes the list sound as it did in the original city, a deliberate show of weakness in a place that admired strength.
views: The appeal is to the whole church
A common reading: 6:1-2 is addressed to all who have received the grace described in 5:18-21.
The appeal is to the rebels
A few read 'do not receive God's grace in vain' as aimed at the group still unsure of Paul, with the severe letter and the offender in the background.

settings.when: at the end of the hardships list, before the command about separation
settings.why: to ask for their affection in return. He has spoken openly and given them room in his heart; they are the ones holding back. The tender tone matters for reading 6:14-18: if this is where Paul stops asking for love, the next verses are the warning of a father, not a general rule.

settings.what: The command about the mismatched yoke
settings.by: Paul (in the unity view); an earlier writer or a Jewish source (in the interpolation views)
settings.to: the church at Corinth, whose members still lived, worked and often married among pagans, and who had been told in 1 Corinthians to flee idol feasts
settings.when: unknown if it is an earlier piece; in the unity view, written with the rest of chapters 1-7
settings.why: to call the church to give its undivided loyalty to God. The question is what the 'yoke' is. The Corinthian letters suggest it is the worship of idols and a share in pagan temple meals, not all contact with outsiders (1 Corinthians 5:9-10; 7:12-16; 10:27). A reader who takes 'unbelievers' as 'everyone outside the church' changes the meaning from a call to exclusive worship to a call to isolation.
views: Paul wrote it for Corinth, to complete the argument that began with 1 Corinthians 10: no sharing in idol worship (Webb; Fee's article title says it is about food offered to idols).
Paul wrote it on another occasion, or took over a Jewish or Jewish-Christian text, and it stands here as his own use of it; the first audience of the original piece is then unknown.
The paragraph came from another occasion or another writer and was placed here later; its first audience is unknown (Betz asked whether it is an anti-Pauline fragment).

traditions.q: How do churches apply 'do not be yoked with unbelievers' to marriage and partnership with non-Christians?
views: These sources deal with marriage law; they are not a commentary on 6:14, and this card does not claim the Church reads the verse only as a marriage rule. Marriage between a Catholic and a baptized non-Catholic needs the bishop's permission, and marriage to an unbaptized person needs a dispensation from 'disparity of cult'; the Church teaches that such marriages bring special difficulties, and also that the validity of the marriage is not in doubt if the rules are met (Catechism 1633-1637; Code of Canon Law, canons 1086 and 1124-1129).

Canon 72 of the Council in Trullo does not permit an orthodox man to marry a heretical woman or an orthodox woman to marry a heretical man. The canon is marriage law; this card does not show that it rests on 6:14.

The Westminster Confession says Christians should 'marry in the Lord' and not marry unbelievers, papists or idolaters (24.3). The proof texts printed with Westminster 24.3 include 2 Corinthians 6:14 (cited with 'see'), so this confession ties the verse to marriage; it has been applied from there to other close ties.

The Schleitheim Confession (1527), article 4, calls for separation from 'the abomination' and from the evil the devil planted in the world, including oaths sworn in unbelief and weapons of force; it echoes the pairs of 6:14-16 (Christ and Belial, God's temple and idols) but cites no verse.

No Baptist confession speaks to this verse, and no source is cited here. The two readings below are typical teaching, not an official position: many teach that the text forbids a Christian to marry or enter a binding partnership with an unbeliever; others point out that Paul tells a believer married to an unbeliever to stay (1 Corinthians 7:12-14) and read 6:14 mainly as a call to avoid idol worship.

title: Grief, Repentance and the Joy of Titus
sum: Chapter 7 closes the call of 6:14-18 (verse 1) and then returns to the story broken off at 2:13. Paul had left Troas in distress because Titus did not come. Now Titus has come, and the news is good: the Corinthians were sorry, they punished the wrong, and they long to see Paul (7:5-7). His severe letter hurt them, and he first regretted sending it. Now he does not (7:8-9).

The center of the chapter is a short lesson on grief. Grief in God's way leads to repentance and a salvation no one regrets; the grief of the world only leads to death (7:10). Paul lists what the right kind of grief produced in the church: eagerness, a defense, anger, fear, longing, zeal, and justice (7:11). The chapter ends in joy and confidence (7:13-16). It is the hinge of the letter: from here Paul can ask for money (8-9).
readings: Read as a reconciliation report

Chapters 1-7 tell, in Paul's own mixed order, how the break with Corinth was mended: the plan change (1:15-2:4), the painful visit and severe letter (2:1-11), the wait at Troas (2:12-13), Titus's arrival (7:5-7). Chapter 7 is the happy ending, and everything before it about ministry leads here.
Read as a lesson on repentance

The chapter is the Bible's most compact teaching on the difference between regret and repentance (7:8-11). Readers across the churches have taken it as a model for pastoral care: say the hard thing, wait, and receive the sorrow that follows.
Read as a diplomat's letter

Paul's praise is generous and pointed. He tells the Corinthians what he said to Titus about them (7:14) so that they will be what he said they were. A letter that praises people in order to move them is an old form, and Paul's mix of warmth and pressure here looks ahead to the collection in chapters 8-9.

views.H: Paul is in Macedonia. Titus has just come from Corinth, where he had carried the severe letter. The story: 1 Corinthians (Ephesus) -> unrest in Corinth -> a short 'painful visit' by Paul (2:1) -> the severe letter carried by Titus (2:3-4; 7:8) -> Paul leaves Ephesus, waits at Troas, goes to Macedonia (2:12-13; 7:5) -> Titus returns with good news (7:6-7) -> 2 Corinthians.
views.C: Where did the painful visit and severe letter fall? Views: a lost letter, 1 Corinthians, or chapters 10-13 (the partition theories). If the severe letter is 10-13, chapter 7 describes the effect of a letter that comes later in our text, which many find hard. If it is lost, the 'wrongdoer' of 7:12 may be a man who insulted Paul, or the man of 1 Corinthians 5:1. The textual variants at 7:12 and 7:13 are pronoun swaps. The connection between 2:13 and 7:5 has made some think the intervening 2:14-7:4 was inserted; others reply that Paul simply holds his readers in suspense.
views.L: The structure is a chiasm in miniature: grief (7:8-9a), repentance (9b-10), the fruits of repentance (11), purpose of the letter (12), and the joy of Titus (13-16). The word play on 'regret' and 'repentance' (7:8-10) and the seven-fold list in 7:11 (the first item introduced by 'what' and the next six by 'yes') are among the finest rhetorical moments in the letter. The language of boasting returns at 7:14 and sets up chapters 8-9, where Paul boasts about the Corinthians to the Macedonians and about the Macedonians to the Corinthians.
views.J: The distinction between sorrow that leads to turning and sorrow that does not has a close Jewish parallel in teshuvah, 'return.' Joel 2:12-13 calls for a heart torn and not just clothes, and Psalm 51:17 praises "a broken spirit." Later rabbinic teaching on repentance (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 86a: Rabbi Levi says great is repentance, for it reaches the heavenly throne) shows the same sense that real turning changes the person; Paul's 'repentance without regret' is not unlike it. Paul's call at 7:1 to cleanse oneself from "defilement of flesh and spirit" uses the vocabulary of Israel's purity laws and applies it to the life of the whole person.
views.T: The card shows how the churches describe the grief of 7:10. John Climacus, Ladder of Divine Ascent, step 7, writes of 'joy-making mourning' (charopoion penthos), a near relative of Paul's 'grief in God's way.' Wesley used 7:1 in his teaching on Christian perfection (see the card).

deep.h: The story behind chapters 1-7: visits and letters
deep.b:
Paul's contact with Corinth ran through several steps, and chapter 7 closes the loop. A common reconstruction:

  1. First visit: Paul founds the church (Acts 18:1-18).
  2. A first letter, now lost, about avoiding sexually immoral people (1 Corinthians 5:9).
  3. 1 Corinthians, written from Ephesus.
  4. Second visit (the 'painful visit,' 2:1): a short visit in which someone wronged Paul, and he left hurt (compare 2:5; 7:12).
  5. The severe letter (2:3-4; 7:8): written 'with many tears' and carried by Titus.
  6. Waiting at Troas and Macedonia (2:12-13; 7:5-6) until Titus came with news.
  7. 2 Corinthians (or at least chapters 1-9), from Macedonia.
  8. Third visit planned (12:14; 13:1) and carried out (Acts 20:2-3).

The 'painful visit' is not in Acts, and neither is the lost letter. Acts is a selective book. Some scholars have varied the order; the main point stays: Paul wrote the severe letter in tears, expected the worst, and Titus brought back peace.

deep.h: Regret, repentance and the churches' debate
deep.b: Paul's pair of words, metamelomai (regret) and metanoia (repentance), have been read in different ways. Luther's first of the Ninety-Five Theses says that when Jesus said "Repent," he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance. The Council of Trent, in its chapter on contrition (session 14, chapter 4), speaks of sorrow of mind, hatred of sin committed and the purpose of not sinning again. The card on this chapter sets out how each church describes the grief of 7:10.

echoes: Isaiah 49:13; Psalm 51:17; Joel 2:12-13; Luke 22:61-62; Matthew 27:3-5; 1 Corinthians 5:1-5; 1 Corinthians 5:9; 1 Corinthians 7:14; 2 Corinthians 1:15-2:13; 2 Corinthians 8:1-7

settings.to: the church at Corinth, 'dear friends' (the only 'beloved' of the letter outside 12:19)
settings.when: at the end of the covenant promises of 6:16-18
settings.why: to turn the promises of God's presence, welcome and fatherhood into a task: clean up, carry holiness through to the end. The command rests on what God has done. In the interpolation views it was first aimed at a different community.

settings.to: the church at Corinth: the repentant majority, and any who still stood against Paul
settings.when: in Macedonia, soon after Titus arrived with news of how the severe letter was received
settings.why: to restore the friendship and to prepare for the collection. Paul tells the Corinthians what grief he went through, what joy Titus brought him, and what he said about them to Titus. He praises them in order to bring out the best in them, and he does not yet ask for anything. Knowing that the hardest part of the quarrel is behind him explains why chapters 8-9 can be warm.
views: Chapters 1-9 are one letter written after Titus's return.
Chapters 1-7 and 8-9 may have been sent separately, or chapter 7 follows an earlier 'letter of reconciliation' (some partition theories).

traditions.q: What is the 'godly grief' that leads to repentance (7:10)?
views: The Council of Trent describes contrition as 'sorrow of mind, and a detestation for sin committed, with the purpose of not sinning for the future,' and says that perfect contrition (from love of God) restores the sinner to grace even before the sacrament, while imperfect contrition (attrition, from fear or the ugliness of sin) disposes him to receive it (session 14, chapter 4). Paul's 'godly grief' is read as the beginning of both.

Repentance has two parts: contrition (terrors striking the conscience through knowledge of sin) and faith (born of the gospel and of absolution). It does not earn forgiveness (Augsburg Confession XII). Luther's first of the Ninety-Five Theses says the whole life of believers is to be one of repentance.

Repentance unto life is 'an evangelical grace' (Westminster Confession 15.1). Seeing the danger and the filth of his sins, the sinner turns from them to God, one who 'grieves for, and hates' them (15.2). It is a fruit of faith in Christ and not its cause.

Repentance (metanoia) is a turning of the whole life. John Climacus, Ladder of Divine Ascent, step 7, writes of 'joy-making mourning' (charopoion penthos), a related but different word. It is practiced in confession and across a life of prayer, fasting and almsgiving, not in a single event.
Wesley taught a repentance before faith (conviction of sin) and a 'repentance of believers' after justification, a continuing awareness of remaining sin (sermon 14, 'The Repentance of Believers').

traditions.q: Can a Christian be made perfect in holiness in this life (7:1)?
views: All the faithful are called to the fullness of the Christian life and the perfection of charity (Lumen Gentium 40), which grows by God's grace and cooperation through the sacraments, though Trent holds that no one can avoid all venial sin through life without a special privilege of God (session 6, canon 23).

The goal is union with God (theosis), reached in a lifelong path of purification, illumination and union. Because the end is God himself, it has no limit in this life; no one is called 'perfect' who has stopped growing.
Good works are expected, but they follow faith and do not earn justification (Augsburg Confession VI).

Sanctification is real and grows, but is 'imperfect in this life,' with 'some remnants of corruption' in every part (Westminster Confession 13.2). Paul's 'perfecting holiness' is a lifelong task and a gift, never finished before death.
Wesley taught Christian perfection, which he said is not freedom from ignorance or mistake; his sermon 40, 'Christian Perfection,' quotes 2 Corinthians 7:1 ('perfecting holiness in the fear of God').

title: The Gift for Jerusalem
sum: Paul turns to money. For some years he had been gathering a gift from his Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1-4; Romans 15:25-28). Corinth had started well and then stopped. Paul now holds up the Macedonians, who gave out of "deep poverty" (8:1-5), and asks the Corinthians to finish what they began (8:6-12).

At the center sits one of the best-known sentences in Paul: "You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. He was rich, and yet he became poor for your sake" (8:9). The principle of the chapter is fairness, not a command: from your surplus to their need, and some day the other way round, as in the manna story (8:13-15). The chapter ends with a recommendation of Titus and two brothers who will handle the money in a way no one can criticize (8:16-24).
readings: Read as a fund-raising letter

Paul praises, compares and nudges: he uses rivalry between provinces, an example, a gentle deadline, and named delegates. Read this way, 8-9 is a lesson in how a leader asks without commanding (8:8, 10).
Read as theology of grace

Money is a means for 'grace' (charis) to move: from God to Macedonia, from Macedonia to Jerusalem, from Jerusalem back in prayer and thanks (9:12-14). The Plain says 'grace' for the eight places where charis means grace (8:1, 4, 6, 7, 9, 19; 9:8, 14), so the pattern stays visible; at 8:16 and 9:15 the same word means 'thanks.'
Read as Jew-Gentile politics

The gift also carried a message. Paul's churches were mostly Gentile; the recipients were Jewish believers who had doubts about them (Galatians 2:10; Romans 15:31). A gift from Gentiles to Jerusalem showed that the two groups were one family (Romans 15:27).

views.H: The Jerusalem church was poor: a famine in Judea (Acts 11:28-30; Josephus, Antiquities 20.2.5, Whiston's numbering) and shared goods (Acts 2:44-45). Macedonia's churches were generous (Philippians 4:15-16). Handling money was a risk: Paul answers with delegates chosen by the churches (8:19-21).
views.C: Are 8 and 9 one letter? Chapter 9 starts with 'It would be needless for me to write to you about the service for the saints,' which strikes some as odd after a whole chapter on it; Some argue that 9 is a separate letter, perhaps to all Achaia. Defenders of unity note that 9:1 ('for... ') links back to 8:24 and that the repetition is natural in a delicate appeal. Others see 8 and 9 as two parts of the unity of 1-9 with 10-13 as another letter. The textual variants (8:4, 8:7, 8:21) are noted in the text.
views.L: Paul uses the Greek of the Old Testament for his proofs (Exodus 16:18 in 2 Corinthians 8:15; Psalm 112:9, Isaiah 55:10 and Hosea 10:12 in 2 Corinthians 9:9-10). The chapter is built on four exhortations backed by examples: Macedonia (8:1-7), Christ (8:8-9), a plea to finish (8:10-15), and a commendation (8:16-24). Words repeat: charis appears ten times in 8-9 (eight 'grace', two 'thanks'), and 'abound' (perisseuo) runs through both chapters, making the point that God's abundance is the source of theirs. The 'letter of recommendation' (8:16-24) is a known form: the recommended persons are named by their qualities, and the sender vouches for them.
views.J: The gift has Jewish parallels. Exodus 30:11-16 sets a half-shekel payment for the sanctuary; Philo describes offerings gathered in the cities and carried to the temple (Special Laws 1.76-78); and Torah commands care for the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Leviticus 19:9-10). Some scholars see in Paul's collection the biblical hope that the nations would bring gifts to Zion (Isaiah 60:5-7) and read it as a sign of the last days. Others find in it a plainer aim: relief for the poor and a bond between Jew and Gentile. Paul uses both ideas.
views.T: A parallel to 8:9, though not a comment on it, is Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54: 'He was made man that we might be made God.' Wesley's rule 'gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can' (The Use of Money, sermon 50) is a Protestant echo of chapters 8-9. Some modern churches read the chapter as the biblical model for stewardship campaigns, and others warn against using 8:9 to promise wealth (see the note).

deep.h: Why did Paul collect money for Jerusalem? Four views
deep.b:
1. Relief for the poor. The Jerusalem leaders asked Paul to "remember the poor," which he was eager to do (Galatians 2:10). The famine and the church's shared goods explain the need (Acts 11:28-30; 2:44-45).

2. A sign of unity. Paul calls the gift a koinonia (a 'sharing') and says that the Gentiles owe it because they have shared in Jerusalem's spiritual things (Romans 15:26-27). It tells the church in Jerusalem that Gentile believers are family. Paul's fear that the gift might not be "acceptable to the saints" (Romans 15:31) shows how much was at stake.

3. The offering of the nations. Some scholars read the collection against the prophets who said that the nations would stream to Zion with gifts (Isaiah 2:2-3; 60:5-7; 66:20). Paul, on this view, was bringing the first fruits of the nations to the Temple city as a sign that the last days had begun (compare Romans 15:16, where the Gentiles become "an offering God welcomes"). Downs (2008) titled his study of the collection The Offering of the Gentiles. Paul never quotes these prophets in 2 Corinthians 8-9.

4. Paul's own strategy. Some scholars think Paul also hoped the gift would win support for his mission in Jerusalem, where he had enemies. Paul's fear in Romans 15:30-31 fits this.

These views are not rivals; the gift may have had several purposes at once. What is not in dispute is that it mattered enormously to Paul: he planned his last journey to Jerusalem around it, and that journey led to his arrest (Acts 21:17-36; 24:17).

deep.h: How Paul asks: nine principles in 8:1-9:15
deep.b:
1. It is grace, not a tax (8:1, 4, 6-7, 19).
  2. It is voluntary (8:3, 8, 12; 9:7).
  3. It is measured by what a person has (8:12).
  4. It is planned, set aside beforehand (9:5; 1 Corinthians 16:2).
  5. It is based on Christ (8:9).
  6. It is mutual, with a fair balance between givers and receivers (8:13-15).
  7. It is handled openly, by delegates the churches have chosen (8:18-23).
  8. It is for others' need and also produces thanks to God (9:12-14).
  9. It overflows from God's own giving (9:8-11, 15).

Each of these principles is picked up in the cards on giving (chapter 9) and in the church's later teaching on stewardship.

echoes: Exodus 16:18; Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Proverbs 3:4; Isaiah 60:5-7; Acts 11:28-30; Acts 20:4; Acts 24:17; Romans 15:25-31; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4; Galatians 2:10; Philippians 2:6-8; Philippians 4:15-16

settings.what: The appeal to finish the collection
settings.to: the church at Corinth, which had agreed a year earlier to give (8:10; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4)
settings.when: from Macedonia, as Titus prepares to go back to Corinth (8:6, 16-17), in the mid-50s AD
settings.why: to move the Corinthians from a good start to a finished gift, without ordering them (8:8, 10). He holds up the Macedonians and then Christ himself, and he sets a fair rule: out of what you have (8:12). The mention of the Macedonians would have been felt at Corinth, a richer city that valued its standing. The Jerusalem church was the recipient; it was Jewish and poor, and some scholars, reading Galatians 2:10 and Romans 15:31, think it was unsure of Gentile churches.
views: The Corinthians stopped giving because of the quarrel
The usual view: the break with Paul (2:1-11; 7:8-12) put the collection on hold, and now that peace is made he restarts it.
The Corinthians were suspicious of the money
Some argue they feared Paul would use it for himself (12:16-18), and the answer is the committee of 8:18-23.

settings.what: The recommendation of Titus and the two brothers
settings.to: the church at Corinth, which is asked to welcome the delegates. The Macedonian churches, who chose the delegate of 8:19, are named in the letter but are not the ones addressed
settings.when: as the three set out for Corinth with this letter or soon after
settings.why: to introduce the delegates, say why they can be trusted, and give the Corinthians a reason to welcome them. Paul pictures himself as accountable to the churches. In a world where a traveling teacher could be called a fraud (2:17), a letter that names and vouches for the people who carry the money was a practical necessity.

title: Sowing and Reaping: The Cheerful Giver
sum: Chapter 9 says again, in a different way, what chapter 8 has said. Paul has boasted to the Macedonians that Achaia was ready a year ago (9:1-2). He sends the brothers ahead so that the boast does not fall flat and so that the gift is ready "as a blessing and not as greed" (9:3-5).

Then comes the farmer's rule: the one who sows little reaps little, the one who sows much reaps much (9:6). Each should give what he has decided in his heart, not from sorrow or by force, for God loves a glad giver (9:7). God can make every grace overflow so that the givers always have enough to give again (9:8-11). The gift supplies the saints, but its greater fruit is thanks to God and prayers for the givers (9:12-14). The chapter ends in praise: "Thanks to God for his gift that is beyond telling!" (9:15).
readings: Read as a promise of return

Some teachers treat 9:6-10 as a promise that what one gives will come back in kind, in money. Verse 10 says God will "make the fruits of your righteousness grow." On this reading giving is a seed that must be planted to get a harvest.
Read as a call to trust

A common reading takes the chapter as a call to trust God for what is needed to keep giving. The harvest is God's supply (9:8), righteousness (9:10), thanksgiving (9:11-12) and prayers (9:14), and Paul never says the givers will be rich.
Read as worship
The words of 9:12 (leitourgia) and 9:13-15 turn the gift into an offering. The Jerusalem saints praise God, the Corinthians are blessed, and Paul ends not with a command but with thanks.

views.H: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital. Paul had boasted of Achaia's readiness to the Macedonians (9:2) and now fears the shame of showing up with Macedonians and finding the gift unready (9:4). In an honor-and-shame culture this was a serious matter for the givers too. Public giving in Greek cities (euergetism) won honor for donors; Paul redirects the honor to God. The 'brothers' sent ahead are Titus and two others (8:16-24).
views.C: Many scholars have taken 9:1 as the start of a separate letter; others take it as a link to chapter 8 (see the page on chapter 8). The best-known objections: Paul writes as if introducing the subject, repeats the delegates, and treats the Macedonians as a spur (9:2-4) instead of as a model (8:1-5). The reply: the chapter is a second, more pointed round of the same appeal, after chapter 8 has raised the matter. Whether one letter or two, the textual variants at 9:4, 9:5, 9:7 and 9:10 matter little to the sense.
views.L: The chapter turns on a pun between 'blessing' and 'greed' (9:5), then on a chain of three images: sowing and reaping (9:6), God's overflowing grace (9:8) and the farmer's supply of seed and bread (9:10). Notice how 'every' and 'all' (pas) multiply: 'all grace... always all you need... every good work' (9:8). A hymn-like close (9:15) rounds off chapters 8-9, and the word charis, which opens chapter 8 as 'grace' (8:1), closes chapter 9 as 'thanks' (9:15).
views.J: The jump from 'he gave to the poor' to 'his righteousness remains forever' (9:9, Psalm 112:9) leans on a Jewish idea that tzedakah ('righteousness') is giving to the poor. The Mishnah says that kind deeds have no fixed measure (Peah 1:1), and Tobit 12:9 (a work Catholic and Orthodox churches hold as Scripture) says that alms save from death. 'God loves a cheerful giver' also echoes the Greek of Proverbs 22:8a. The Temple tax and the biblical tithes (Leviticus 27:30; Deuteronomy 14:22-29) are the ordinary forms of giving behind Paul's words, though he mentions neither.
views.T: The verse 'God loves a cheerful giver' (9:7) is the best-known text on Christian giving. Cyprian preaches almsgiving as a duty and says the giver's wealth is increased by God's repayment (On Works and Alms, Treatise 8). Churches differ on whether tithing (a tenth) is required of Christians. See the card.

deep.h: One letter, two, or three? Chapters 8 and 9
deep.b:
Paul seems to introduce the collection twice. Chapter 8 introduces it from scratch and uses the Macedonians as a model; chapter 9 begins "It would be needless for me to write to you about the service for the saints" and uses Achaia as the example for the Macedonians. Several theories:

  • Two separate letters (Some scholars): chapter 8 is a letter to Corinth; chapter 9 a circular letter to all the churches of Achaia, sent at about the same time.
  • One letter, one flow Others: 9:1 begins a second part of one appeal, in which Paul turns from persuading to preparing.
  • Part of a letter with 10-13 added later: some hold that 1-9 form one letter and 10-13 another (see the page on chapter 7).

The manuscripts offer no help: all Greek copies carry chapters 8 and 9 together. The decision rests on how one reads Paul's rhetoric. Whichever is right, the content of the appeal is the same.

deep.h: A glad giver and the Greek Old Testament
deep.b: "God loves a cheerful giver" is almost word for word the Greek of Proverbs 22:8a: "God blesses a cheerful and generous man." This line is in the Septuagint and not in the Hebrew Bible, so English Bibles from the Hebrew (and this site's Plain of Proverbs 22:8) do not have it. Paul uses it as Scripture, and the early church did too. The case illustrates a point that matters for the whole letter: the New Testament writers mostly quote the Old Testament in Greek, and the Greek sometimes differs from the Hebrew behind our Old Testaments. Where a New Testament writer relies on the difference, the Plain follows his Greek in his book and notes the difference at the Old Testament verse.

echoes: Proverbs 11:24-25; Proverbs 22:8; Psalm 112:9; Isaiah 55:10; Hosea 10:12; Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Leviticus 27:30; Galatians 6:7-9; Luke 6:38; Romans 15:25-28; Tobit 12:9

settings.to: the church at Corinth (and in the two-letter views, the churches of Achaia)
settings.when: while Macedonian representatives are expected with Paul and the delegates are about to arrive
settings.why: to make sure the gift is ready before Paul and the Macedonians come, so that the Corinthians are not shamed and Paul's boasting is not shown to be empty. The pressure is real: the two provinces are in a friendly contest, and a gift squeezed out at the last moment would count as 'greed,' not as a gift.
views: The chapter was sent to all of Achaia, with chapter 8 for Corinth alone.

settings.what: The farmer's rule and the thanksgiving
settings.when: at the close of the collection appeal
settings.why: to show why giving is not loss. Paul does not threaten and does not promise riches; he says that God gives the giver what is needed to go on giving, and that the gift becomes thanks to God from those who receive it. The first readers were a church with wealthy members and many poor ones; Paul's picture of God supplying seed and bread would have reached both.

traditions.q: Must Christians tithe? What does 'give what you have decided' (9:7) mean?
views: The fifth precept of the Church requires the faithful 'to provide for the needs of the Church' according to their means (Catechism 2043, 2447). Aquinas taught that the duty to support ministers comes partly from natural law, and that under the New Law the fixing of the proportion is left to the ordinance of the Church (Summa II-II, q. 87, a. 1). Almsgiving is a work of mercy and a witness to charity.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 13) says Christians have a 'binding stewardship' of their possessions and should give 'cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally.'

The Fundamental Beliefs of Seventh-day Adventists (belief 21, Stewardship) say believers acknowledge God's ownership by faithful service and by "returning tithes and giving offerings for the proclamation of His gospel and the support and growth of His church."
Wesley's rule in 'The Use of Money' (sermon 50) was to gain all one can, save all one can and give all one can.
